title: Invoice Payment Dual Approval for Restaurant Chains: How to End the Director Bottleneck
summary: Stop directors from logging in twice to approve invoices and payments. Learn how F&B chains automate dual-approval workflows for high-value transactions.
body_text: TL;DR: Restaurant chains that require director approval for both invoices and payment runs above a certain threshold are burning hundreds of hours a year on manual double-logins. Automated dual-approval workflows — triggered by configurable amount thresholds — route invoices and payment batches through a single, unified web-based approval interface, eliminating redundant ERP logins, cutting payment cycle times, and giving finance directors complete visibility without the friction. The Problem Nobody Talks About in F&B Finance Picture a finance team at a restaurant group running 26 locations across a major metro. Four finance staff are managing supplier invoices, staff expense claims, and payment runs for every outlet. The process works — until an invoice crosses a certain dollar threshold. At that point, the finance team’s director must log into the ERP system to approve the invoice. Then, when the payment run is prepared, the director must log in again to authorize the payment. Two separate system sessions, two separate approval actions, for the same transaction. The finance team’s own words describe the confusion well: “So if my director needs to approve the invoice and approve the payments, he will go into the system twice?” The answer from their finance manager: “Yeah, some of that because the amount is over a certain amount.” This is the reality of invoice payment dual approval in food and beverage businesses — a control that exists for good reason, executed in the most friction-heavy way possible. And it’s costing multi-outlet restaurant chains far more than anyone realizes. For finance teams already stretched thin across dozens of outlets, approval workflow bottlenecks created by manual dual-approval processes directly delay vendor payments, strain supplier relationships, and eat into the director’s working hours on tasks that should take seconds, not sessions. Why Do Restaurant Chains Require Directors to Approve Both Invoice and Payment? The dual-approval requirement is not arbitrary. It exists because of two well-established financial controls that are especially important in high-transaction-volume businesses like restaurant groups. Separation of Duties Separation of duties (SoD) is a core internal control principle. It means no single person should control all parts of a financial transaction — from receiving an invoice to authorizing payment. In a restaurant chain context, this typically means: Outlet manager submits an expense or vendor invoice Finance team reviews, codes the GL, and prepares the payment batch Director or CFO approves the invoice (confirming it’s legitimate) Director or CFO authorizes the payment run (confirming the money should go out) The logic is sound. But when the approval authority for both stages sits with the same person and the tool requires two separate logins to execute both, the process becomes operationally painful rather than a genuine control. Threshold-Based Risk Controls Restaurant groups processing hundreds of supplier invoices monthly often apply risk tiers. Low-value invoices — weekly produce deliveries, cleaning supplies — may auto-approve or go through a junior-level sign-off. Higher-value invoices — kitchen equipment, renovation contracts, bulk liquor orders — trigger an escalation to the director. This tiered approach makes sense from a risk management perspective. According to the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners’ Report to the Nations , organizations with fewer controls over high-value transactions suffer significantly higher fraud losses — median losses for billing schemes exceed $100,000 per incident. Requiring director review on high-value invoices is a genuine safeguard. The problem is not the control. The problem is the execution: an ERP-based system that forces the director to log in, navigate menus, find the invoice, approve it, log out — and then repeat the entire process again when the payment is batched. This is AP automation done halfway. What Are the Hidden Costs of Director Dual-Approval Bottlenecks in F&B? The double-login problem sounds like a minor inconvenience. It is not. For restaurant chains operating on thin margins with complex vendor relationships and high invoice volumes, the cumulative cost is significant. 1. Payment Delays Damage Vendor Relationships When director approval is required before a payment run can proceed, any delay — the director is traveling, in meetings, unavailable — holds up payment to multiple vendors simultaneously. A payment batch that should go out Tuesday slips to Thursday or Friday. Across a restaurant chain with dozens of active suppliers, these delays accumulate. Strained vendor relationships in F&B have direct operational consequences. A produce supplier who consistently receives late payments will deprioritize your chain’s orders during peak seasons. A beverage distributor managing tight stock may stop extending credit terms. Vendor payment optimization is not just a finance metric — in restaurants, it directly affects what goes on the menu. 2. Director Time Is Not Free A director approving invoices one by one, then approving payment batches in a separate session, may spend 60–90 minutes per week purely navigating ERP interfaces to perform approvals. Over 50 working weeks, that is between 50 and 75 hours annually — roughly two working weeks — consumed by friction that automation should eliminate entirely. For a leadership-level role, this is expensive time poorly spent. Finance directors should be reviewing exceptions and making judgment calls, not performing mechanical logins. 3. Manual Processes Create Duplicate Payment Risk When approval processes are slow or fragmented, finance teams sometimes submit invoices or payment requests multiple times to “nudge” an approval through the system. Duplicate submissions, if not caught, result in duplicate payments — a common and costly error that affects restaurants with high-volume, repeat supplier invoices. 4. Staff at Outlets Are Left in the Dark In a 26-outlet restaurant group, kitchen managers and outlet supervisors submit invoices and expense claims without visibility into where their submissions stand in the approval chain. They cannot see if the invoice is pending director review, stuck in the finance team’s queue, or already paid. This leads to repeated follow-ups, duplicate submissions, and avoidable frustration for field staff. The mobile accessibility limitations of legacy ERP approval tools compound this problem for staff who are rarely at a desktop. 5. Budget Visibility Gaps Accumulate Across Outlets With invoice approvals and payment authorizations split across two separate workflow steps — and no unified dashboard — finance teams struggle to track committed spend versus approved payments in real time. Budget control and visibility gaps that arise from manual tracking make it difficult to reconcile what was invoiced, what was approved, and what was paid at the outlet level. How to Fix the Director Dual-Approval Bottleneck in Restaurant Chains This is a solvable problem. Here is a step-by-step approach to eliminating the dual-login bottleneck while preserving the underlying control logic that makes dual approval necessary. Step 1: Map Your Current Approval Stages Before automating anything, document every step in your current process: Who submits invoices and claims (outlet managers, kitchen staff)? What is the dollar threshold that triggers director-level approval? Are invoice approval and payment authorization always required for the same person, or can they be delegated independently? Which ERP or accounting system (SAP B1, Xero, QuickBooks, NetSuite) does your team currently use? This mapping reveals where delays actually occur — and which approval steps can be consolidated without reducing control quality. Step 2: Implement a Web-Based Submission Layer for Outlets Replace manual invoice submission (email, paper, ERP portal) with a web-based submission form that outlet managers and field staff can access from any device. Staff should be able to submit invoices or expense claims by uploading a document, entering key details, and submitting — without needing ERP credentials. A web-based submission layer removes the access barrier for non-finance staff and creates a clean digital audit trail from the moment an invoice enters your system. Step 3: Configure Threshold-Based Routing Rules Set up configurable routing rules that automatically escalate invoices based on dollar amount: Below threshold (e.g., under HKD 10,000): routed to finance team for coding and payment preparation Above threshold: automatically flagged for director-level invoice approval before payment preparation begins Critically, these routing rules should be set once and applied consistently — not manually assigned by the finance team for each invoice. Step 4: Unify Invoice Approval and Payment Authorization in One Interface This is the key step that eliminates the double-login problem. Rather than having the director approve the invoice in one system session and the payment batch in another, a unified approval dashboard should: Surface both the pending invoice approval and the corresponding payment authorization in a single view Allow the director to review invoice details, GL coding, and payment amount in one place Approve both actions sequentially in the same session — or, where controls allow, configure a single approval action that satisfies both requirements This does not weaken the separation of duties. The finance team still prepares the payment batch separately. The director still approves both the invoice legitimacy and the payment authorization. But the director does it in one workflow session instead of two. Step 5: Enable Mobile-First Approval for Directors Directors at multi-outlet F&B groups are rarely at a desk when invoices need approval. An approval workflow that only works via desktop ERP will always create delays. Configure mobile-friendly approval notifications — via email or a mobile app — that allow directors to review invoice details and approve or reject from their phone without logging into an ERP system. Step 6: Integrate Back to Your ERP for Payment Execution Once the director approves the payment run, the authorized payment file should be automatically generated in a format compatible with your ERP (SAP B1, NetSuite, Xero) or exported as a GIRO/bank upload file. This eliminates the manual step of re-entering approved payments into the accounting system. What Does Automated Dual-Approval Look Like for F&B Finance Teams? A modern AP approval workflow built for restaurant chains looks fundamentally different from a legacy ERP approval screen. Unified Approval Dashboard Instead of separate approval queues for invoices and payment runs, the director sees a single dashboard: invoices pending first-level approval, payment batches awaiting final authorization, and a complete history of what was approved, by whom, and when. Everything in one place. Threshold-Based Auto-Routing Amount thresholds are configured once. When an invoice comes in above the defined limit, the system routes it to the director automatically — no manual flagging by the finance team required. When it falls below the threshold, it moves through the standard finance team review flow. Smart Batching for Payment Authorization Rather than asking the director to authorize each payment individually, the system batches all approved invoices into a single payment run for director sign-off. The director reviews the batch summary — total amount, vendor list, individual invoice breakdown — and approves the entire run in one action. ERP Sync Without Manual Re-Entry Once the payment batch is authorized, the approved data syncs directly to your ERP or generates a ready-to-upload payment file. No manual re-entry, no transcription errors, no additional ERP login needed. Full Audit Trail Every approval action — who approved, at what time, at what amount, against which invoice — is logged automatically. This creates a complete audit trail for internal controls, external audit, and compliance review without any additional documentation effort from the finance team. How Peakflo Solves the Dual-Approval Problem for Restaurant Chains Peakflo’s accounts payable automation platform is built specifically to handle the kind of multi-outlet, multi-threshold approval complexity that restaurant groups deal with daily. Configurable Approval Policies : Set amount thresholds, approval tiers, and escalation rules that reflect your actual business logic — not generic workflow templates. A 26-outlet restaurant group can configure different approval chains for different expense categories, outlet sizes, or vendor types. Web-Based Submission for Field Staff : Outlet managers and kitchen supervisors submit invoices and claims through a simple web interface — no ERP credentials, no desktop required. Submissions are automatically queued for finance team review and director approval based on your configured rules. Unified Invoice + Payment Approval Interface : Directors review and approve both invoice legitimacy and payment authorization from a single dashboard — accessible from desktop or mobile. No double login. No navigating separate ERP menus. The control is preserved; the friction is eliminated. Mobile Approval Notifications : Directors receive approval requests via email or mobile notification with full invoice details attached. They can approve, reject, or request clarification directly from their device — without accessing an ERP system. ERP Integration and Payment File Export : Peakflo integrates with SAP Business One, Xero, QuickBooks, and other accounting systems used by F&B operators. Approved payment runs generate files ready for direct upload to your ERP or bank payment system, removing manual re-entry from the process entirely. Real-Time Spend Visibility : Finance teams and directors can see committed invoices, pending approvals, and authorized payments in real time — giving them the budget visibility that manual processes simply cannot provide. According to a Deloitte Digital Finance study , finance teams that automate approval workflows reduce invoice processing time by up to 70% and cut payment cycle times by more than half. For a 26-outlet restaurant group running thousands of invoices annually, those gains translate directly into cash flow improvement and vendor relationship quality. Frequently Asked Questions What is invoice payment dual approval in restaurant chains? Invoice payment dual approval is a financial control process where high-value transactions require the same senior approver — typically a finance director or CFO — to separately authorize both the invoice (confirming it is legitimate and correctly coded) and the payment run (confirming the funds should be disbursed). This two-stage control exists to enforce separation of duties and reduce fraud risk on large transactions. In manual ERP-based systems, it requires two separate system logins, creating unnecessary friction and payment delays. At what amount threshold should a restaurant chain require director-level dual approval? The threshold varies by business size, risk appetite, and jurisdiction. Restaurant groups typically set thresholds based on their average transaction size and vendor payment patterns. Common configurations include tiered thresholds — for example, invoices above a certain amount require finance manager approval, while invoices above a higher amount require director or CFO approval for both the invoice and payment authorization. The key is that thresholds should be set intentionally, documented in your internal control policy, and enforced automatically through your AP system rather than applied case-by-case. Can automating dual approval weaken internal controls? No — when implemented correctly, automation strengthens internal controls. Automated dual-approval workflows enforce your approval policies consistently on every transaction, with no exceptions or manual overrides. Every approval action is logged with a timestamp, user identity, and transaction details, creating a more complete audit trail than manual processes. The separation of duties between finance team preparation and director authorization is preserved; the only thing that changes is the elimination of redundant ERP logins. How does Peakflo integrate with ERP systems used by F&B companies? Peakflo integrates with the ERP systems commonly used by F&B operators — including SAP Business One, Oracle NetSuite, and QuickBooks — through structured integrations that sync vendor master data, invoice records, and GL coding. Invoices approved and payment-authorized in Peakflo can be exported as ERP-compatible files for upload or pushed directly to your ERP via the integration layer. This eliminates the need for finance teams to manually re-enter approved payment data, reducing transcription errors and saving significant time on every payment cycle. Conclusion: The Double Login Is a Design Flaw, Not a Control Requiring a restaurant chain’s director to log into an ERP system twice — once to approve an invoice and once to authorize the payment — is not a financial control. It is a design flaw in how that control is implemented. The underlying policy (dual sign-off on high-value transactions) is sound. The execution (two separate sessions, two manual navigations, two logins) is not. F&B operators running multiple outlets cannot afford the payment delays, vendor relationship strain, and director time drain that come with manual dual-approval processes. As transaction volumes scale with outlet count, the problem compounds. Modern AP automation platforms like Peakflo give restaurant chains a better path: configurable threshold-based routing, unified invoice and payment approval in a single web-based interface, mobile-first approvals for directors in the field, and clean ERP sync that eliminates manual re-entry. The control is preserved. The friction is removed. If your finance director is still logging in twice, it is time to fix that. title: Adventure Starts Just Outside Your Front Door at The Townes at Willow Park
body_text: Adventure Starts Just Outside Your Front Door at The Townes at Willow Park Tri Pointe Homes • August 13, 2026 Share this article Homebuyers are looking for more than just square footage; they want places to bike, walk, unwind, and connect with nature and each other. Lucky for them, The Townes at Willow Park by Tri Pointe Homes® makes nature your backyard. Here, you’re surrounded by some of the Triangle’s best parks, greenways and trails. Whether it’s a morning walk, weekend hike or even an afternoon on the water, outdoor adventure is never more than a few miles away. Read on to explore some of the nearby parks and trails that give residents of The Townes at Willow Park room to connect with nature well beyond their own doorstep. William B. Umstead State Park Located just seven miles from The Townes at Willow Park via its Reedy Creek Entrance , William B. Umstead State Park is much more than a county park or greenway. It takes outdoor exploration to the next level with more than 5,000 acres of protected forests, lakes and trails just waiting to be discovered. As one of North Carolina’s most-visited state parks , this natural oasis offers countless ways to take in the state’s scenic beauty. With more than 34 miles of hiking trails and 13 miles of multi-use trails open to both biking and horseback riding, this park offers ways to enjoy the outdoors in every season. Visitors can also experience paddling across the park’s lakes, casting a line while fishing or gathering with loved ones to enjoy a meal at one of the many picnic areas. For those looking to extend their time in the great outdoors, William B. Umstead State Park offers overnight camping options equipped with tent sites, group camping areas, firewood and bathhouses. These overnight accommodations allow visitors to fully immerse themselves in the park and all that it has to offer. Beyond camping, visitors can take advantage of the educational opportunities the park provides at the visitor center where exhibits are offered to learn more about the area’s natural and cultural history. For residents of The Townes at Willow Park, having a true North Carolina state jewel like William B. Umstead State Park just seven miles from home means an immersive outdoor escape is always close by. Morrisville Community Park Not every outdoor destination near The Townes at Willow Park is designed for an all-day-and-night adventure. Nearby parks and greenways provide residents with convenient opportunities to enjoy nature as part of their everyday routine. Less than 2.5 miles from home, Morrisville Community Park combines outdoor recreation with easy access to the surrounding community. Featuring athletic fields, playgrounds, picnic shelters, tennis and pickleball courts, outdoor fitness equipment and direct access to the Hatcher Creek Greenway , the park offers something for everyone. Beyond its outdoor perks, Morrisville Community Park’s convenient location puts residents close to the shopping and dining options that make the area so desirable. Nearby destinations like Park West Village offer a variety of local favorites, from picking up fresh groceries at Trader Joe’s to browsing the latest finds at Nordstrom Rack. After a morning on the greenway or at the playground works up an appetite or a big win on the softball field calls for a team celebration, Willow Park residents can easily head over to nearby favorites like Another Broken Egg Café or Ruckus Pizza, Pasta and Spirits to enjoy a meal together. With outdoor recreation, shopping and dining all within easy reach, residents can make the most of their day by enjoying the park, checking off their to-do list and creating memories throughout the community. Lake Crabtree County Park Just minutes from The Townes at Willow Park, Lake Crabtree County Park hosts guests with a wide range of interests. The park is built around a 520-acre lake, and seasonal boat rentals bring kayaks, canoes, stand-up paddleboards and pedal boats within easy reach. Anglers can cast from a boat or from the fishing pier. On land, the six-mile Lake Trail follows the shoreline, with its eastern stretch connecting to the Black Creek Greenway. That stretch is open to bikes, while the short Old Beech Nature Trail offers a walking loop with a trailside brochure that explains what you're looking at. Add playgrounds, picnic areas and open play fields to the list, and it is easy to spend a full afternoon here. Whether residents want an active morning on the water or a peaceful walk surrounded by trees, Lake Crabtree County Park is an easy escape close to home. Having that kind of open space a few minutes away means a change of scenery never takes much planning. Cedar Fork District Park Also less than 2.5 miles from The Townes at Willow Park, Cedar Fork District Park is 37 acres of wide open green space. Eight multi-use fields host soccer, football, lacrosse and other field sports, and when nothing is scheduled, that same open ground works just as well for a frisbee, a long walk or a picnic under one of the shelters. The grounds are open sunrise to sunset, which makes it an easy stop whether the plan is a Saturday game or just an hour outside after work. Hatcher Creek Greenway If the parks are the destinations, the greenway is what strings them together. Hatcher Creek Greenway runs about 2.5 miles of paved trail through Morrisville, the longest greenway in the town, and residents can pick it up at Morrisville Community Park a couple of miles from home. From there it runs toward Crabtree Creek and feeds into the wider network of greenways that reaches Lake Crabtree and continues on toward William B. Umstead State Park. Connectivity is key! A morning that starts as a short walk can just as easily turn into a long ride out to the lake, and it is what makes the outdoors around The Townes at Willow Park feel far bigger than any single park on a map. Find Your Home at The Townes at Willow Park State park trails, a 520-acre lake and neighborhood greenways all sit within a short drive, which means the outdoors is part of everyday life here rather than something to plan a trip around. Pair that with low-maintenance townhome living and a location that keeps Research Triangle Park, Raleigh-Durham International Airport and Park West Village close at hand, and a weekend adventure can start right outside the front door. title: The Most Valuable Database in Construction Is the One You Already Own
summary: Running construction projects is complicated. We make it simple.
body_text: Insight Most construction companies have delivered hundreds of projects. Every new bid still tends to begin with the same manual hunt for risks, prices, and lessons the company already paid to learn. The same risks resurface, the same questions go back to the client, and estimators dig for old prices while a project manager tries to recall what went wrong last time. The knowledge exists, but it's scattered across finished project folders, old estimates, change order logs, meeting minutes, email threads, and the memory of colleagues. When it can't be found at the right moment, every project starts further back than it should. Why the Lesson Rarely Reaches the Next Bid A single lesson is often split across three places. The issue sits in meeting minutes, the cost sits in the estimate, and the consequence sits in a change order log. Seeing the whole picture means finding all three, and when a bid is due there is rarely time to read years of history. So teams work from what they remember or happen to stumble on, and knowledge stays tied to individuals instead of the organisation. Making old documents searchable helps, but a search bar alone falls short. The relevant detail might be a comment in an old estimate, a line in an appendix, or one sentence in meeting minutes. To be useful, the system has to understand context and connect a clause in the new tender to a comparable situation from before, such as the same contract model, similar ground conditions, or a requirement that once triggered an expensive change. From Archive to Project Memory Brickanta's Knowledge Base turns finished projects into reference material for new analysis. It reads past estimates, contracts, change order logs, and final reports, then makes that history available while a new bid package is under review. When AI Documents analyses a bid package and finds a responsibility clause on temporary works, the Knowledge Base can show that a near-identical clause led to an unpriced cost on two earlier jobs, pull the change order records behind it, and suggest the question worth asking the client before submission. Every job has its own conditions, and the estimator or lawyer judges what actually compares. The agent won't decide that two projects are the same, but it puts relevant history on the table. History Is Only Useful If You Can Verify It Telling a team that a clause caused problems in a previous project isn't enough on its own. Every finding in Brickanta traces back to its source, so an estimator can move from a recommendation to the exact change order entry or final report behind it and decide whether the experience fits the new job. A flag without a source only adds more uncertainty. This matters most when people move on. An experienced estimator carries years of pattern recognition, knowing which clauses deserve a second look and which risks tend to get underestimated. When they leave, the documents stay, but the ability to find the right one and connect it to a new project can walk out with them. A shared project memory keeps more of that inside the company. Every project is unique, and none of them should have to start from zero. Your next bid should benefit from every project your organisation has already finished. Request a demo see how Brickanta turns your project history into a searchable, verifiable knowledge base.

title: Patent Search Price: Costs by Search Type in 2026
summary: Patent search prices range from free DIY tools to five-figure legal opinions. Compare patentability, invalidity, FTO, AI, and USPTO search costs.
body_text: Back to insights Patent Search Price: Costs by Search Type in 2026 August 18, 2026 &AI Team An illustrative $99 patent-search quote and a $25,000 freedom-to-operate opinion can both be fair for their stated scopes. They buy different work. The word “search” hides differences in the question, sources, claim analysis, jurisdiction, and attorney review. Those differences determine whether a quote is useful or merely cheap. A sound budget starts with current price benchmarks, the deliverable included at each tier, and a scope that excludes analysis you do not need. Patent search prices at a glance Start with the decision the search must support. A patentability search looks for prior art that may affect a proposed invention’s novelty or nonobviousness. An invalidity search looks for prior art against one or more issued claims. A freedom-to-operate (FTO) search looks for enforceable claims that may cover a planned product or activity. A landscape maps a broader technology field. The same patent database may appear in all four workflows. The documents selected, date rules, legal-status work, and final deliverable are different. All dollar amounts are U.S. dollars. Amounts marked € are euros. What you are buying Indicative published price or usage allocation What the cited example establishes DIY preliminary search $0 in database fees No paid service is included. You perform the keyword, classification, citation, patent, and non-patent literature review. Our Prior Art Search Our pricing page reports a 176-credit average over the 90 days measured as of July 2026. That usage is $70.40 pay as you go. Monthly Pro is $625 per user per month and includes 2,500 credits; 176 credits have an effective allocation of $44 within that commitment. Annual Pro is $6,000 per user per year and includes 30,000 credits; $35.20 is the effective allocation of 176 credits within that commitment. Our product FAQ separately says searches typically cost $100–$300 in credits ( pricing basis ; product FAQ ) We return ranked references with pinpoint passages or figures, support iterative refinement, and let users chart or export results. Attorney review is separate, and none of these figures is a fixed per-search promise. Search-only novelty or patentability search $400–$1,400 ( published average prices ) Planet Patent calls these average prices for a tailored report and provides a firm quote only after reviewing the request. Confirm sources, jurisdictions, analysis, and report format in the quote. Patentability search with attorney opinion $1,500–$2,300 ( published fees ; fixed-fee example ) Axenfeld lists a patent search, detailed patentability opinion, result discussion, and options for moving forward. Simpson & Simpson lists a preliminary novelty search and opinion. Neither example prices application drafting or claim strategy as part of the package. Invalidity search $1,900–$10,000 ( published average range ) Planet Patent says its service tests patent strength by comparing claims against prior art and active patents. Confirm claim count, governing date work, sources, mappings, and report format in the quote. FTO or clearance search Planet Patent lists $1,500–$3,000 ( published average range ). The Finnish Patent and Registration Office (PRH) charges €2,670 base plus a mandatory €6.50 invoicing charge, both subject to 25.5% value-added tax (VAT), and shows €3,359 total for its standard scope ( PRH service ; fee schedule ) Planet Patent says its FTO or clearance search includes an infringement search and a review of expired patents. PRH’s standard scope includes an initial meeting, about two days of examiner search work, a report with legal-status information, and copies of the ten most relevant publications. PRH does not give an infringement conclusion. Formal FTO legal opinion $10,000–$30,000 ( 2017 law-firm guidance ) Morse describes a formal opinion addressing whether a product or service infringes issued patents and notes the time required to review patents and construe potentially conflicting claims. Confirm the preceding search scope and opinion format. Combined FTO search, analysis, and legal opinion $10,000–$50,000+ ( 2026 published estimate ) ipCapital Group separates search and analysis from the legal opinion. It describes a search that identifies potentially blocking patents and maps claims to the product, followed by an attorney’s legal judgment. Its figure is a market estimate, not a rate card. Basic landscape search $800–$1,200 ( published average range ) Planet Patent describes a broad overview of a technology area or industry that includes expired and active patents. Confirm family cleanup, categorization, and analysis depth in the quote. Strategic landscape analysis $5,000–$50,000+ ( published range ) ipCapital Group contrasts a narrow, single-technology review with a broad, multi-jurisdiction competitive landscape. Patent-family count, claim reading, jurisdictions, analytical depth, and requested overlays drive the scope. Treat these as indicative published benchmarks, not universal or typical market rates. Some sources publish average guides, while others publish fixed fees or estimates for a stated engagement. When a provider quotes a fixed price, it usually limits at least one part of the engagement, such as technical scope, jurisdictions, sources, claims, references analyzed, or revision rounds. Complex chemistry, life sciences, semiconductors, standards, and crowded software fields can exceed the upper ranges. The USPTO application search fee is different from a private search The “patent search fee” on a United States Patent and Trademark Office invoice is a government application search fee paid in connection with filing. It is not a standalone patent-search service price and does not purchase a pre-filing report from a searcher or attorney. The agency uses the fee as part of examining the application after filing. The current USPTO fee schedule lists the following domestic application search fees under 37 C.F.R. § 1.16(k) through (m). They apply only to the stated original utility, design or design continuing prosecution application (CPA), and plant categories: Domestic application category Large entity Small entity Micro entity Original utility under § 1.16(k) $770 $308 $154 Design or design CPA under § 1.16(l) $300 $120 $60 Plant under § 1.16(m) $485 $194 $97 For an application in one of these § 1.16 categories, the search fee is due in addition to the applicable basic filing fee and examination fee. A provisional application has a filing fee but no separate § 1.16 search or examination fee. The table does not cover every nonprovisional filing path. Patent Cooperation Treaty national-stage applications, for example, use a separate fee framework under 37 C.F.R. § 1.492. Reissue applications have a separate search-fee category under § 1.16(n). These distinctions explain why a search quote from counsel can appear alongside a second “search fee” on the government-fee estimate without being a duplicate charge. What you get at each price tier Free DIY search: database access costs nothing, judgment takes time USPTO Patent Public Search, Google Patents, Espacenet, and the World Intellectual Property Organization’s (WIPO) PATENTSCOPE provide free access to large patent collections. The USPTO’s own six-step search strategy begins with brainstorming terms and running keyword searches. It then calls for reviewing found documents in depth, expanding through relevant Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) classes, reviewing cited and citing references, and broadening the search to foreign patents, non-patent literature, or a patent professional’s search. That is much more work than typing a product name into one search box. A preliminary DIY search is useful for finding a clear knockout reference and learning the vocabulary used in the field. Its cash price is $0, but its true cost is the time required to build queries, read the specification and claims, group patent families, and change direction as new terminology appears. It also has unavoidable limits. U.S. prior art can include patents, published applications, printed publications, public use, sales, and other public availability under 35 U.S.C. § 102 . Patent-only searching leaves part of that universe untouched. Most U.S. nonprovisional utility and plant applications are published around 18 months from the earliest filing date for which a benefit is sought, subject to the exceptions in 35 U.S.C. § 122(b)(2). Applications that remain unpublished create an unpublished-application blind spot that a paid search cannot remove either. For a claim governed by the first-inventor-to-file provisions of the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act (AIA), a U.S. patent document that publishes or issues later may still qualify as § 102(a)(2) prior art. It must name another inventor, have been effectively filed before that claim’s effective filing date for the relied-on subject matter, and fall outside the § 102(b)(2) exceptions. AI-assisted search: our 176-credit average and $100–$300 FAQ range AI search products charge per report, credit, user, or annual license. That makes a single market-wide per-search range misleading. The price gap matters less than the output gap. A useful AI search should do more than retrieve semantically similar abstracts. For patent work, look for: Claim- or limitation-level searching. Patent-family and date information. Pinpoint passages or figures supporting each match. Coverage beyond patents, including non-patent literature when the question calls for it. A visible path from candidate reference to human-reviewed analysis. The ability to revise the search without buying a new report from scratch. We built our Prior Art Search for litigation and post-grant work. Our pricing page reports that a prior art search averaged 176 credits over the 90 days measured as of July 2026. At our posted credit rates, that dated average equals $70.40 pay as you go. Monthly Pro is $625 per user per month and includes 2,500 credits, giving 176 credits an effective allocation of $44 within that commitment. Annual Pro is $6,000 per user per year and includes 30,000 credits, giving 176 credits an effective allocation of $35.20 within that commitment. Those allocations are not standalone search prices. Our pages also give a broader typical range. The Prior Art Search FAQ separately says searches typically cost $100–$300 worth of credits and explains that cost depends on the patent size, the number of results requested, and other factors. The 176-credit number is the pricing page’s dated 90-day average. The $100–$300 figure is the product FAQ’s typical range. Neither benchmark is a fixed price, minimum, cap, or universal per-search promise. Both benchmarks describe platform usage before attorney review. We do not position the output as a pre-filing patentability opinion or an FTO opinion. For litigation teams, the advantage is that search results can move directly into invalidity analysis and a claim chart rather than arriving as an unstructured list of PDFs. Patentability search cost: $400–$1,400, or $1,500–$2,300 with an opinion Published search-only examples span $400–$1,400. Planet Patent’s average-price guide lists $400–$900 for mechanical, electrical, consumer, business-method, electronic, and software novelty searches, and $700–$1,400 for biotech, chemical, genetic, or medical work. These figures are indicative published averages, and Planet Patent provides a firm quote only after reviewing a request. PRH separately charges a €1,265 base fee for its fixed-price novelty search plus a mandatory €6.50 invoicing charge. Both charges are subject to 25.5% VAT under its current fee schedule . Neither source establishes a typical global rate. Published attorney packages provide another useful anchor. Axenfeld Law lists $1,500–$2,000 for a patent search, detailed patentability opinion, and discussion of the result in its service fee . Simpson & Simpson lists $2,200 for most inventions and $2,300 for software and business methods in its fixed-fee example . Those sources do not establish a standard search-only deliverable. In a quote, ask whether the report identifies the closest references, explains their relevance, and states the databases, countries, date range, and non-patent sources covered. The cited attorney examples establish that their stated fees include an opinion. Axenfeld also includes a discussion of the result and options for moving forward. They do not show that added fees necessarily produce more search hits or any particular number of results. Search-only patentability research does not require a registered patent practitioner. A patentability opinion or other legal advice about work contemplated before the USPTO should come from a registered patent attorney or patent agent authorized for that work. The boundary matters. 37 C.F.R. § 11.5 limits USPTO registration to patent matters before the Office and services reasonably necessary and incident to authorized applications or proceedings. Registration does not make a patent agent a licensed attorney. FTO, noninfringement, standalone validity, and litigation opinions outside that scope should be handled by an appropriately licensed attorney. Representing another person or entity in court generally requires counsel admitted to that court. An individual party’s ability to appear pro se depends on applicable law and court rules . USPTO registration alone does not authorize court representation. Read the engagement scope closely. “Patentability analysis” on a low-cost automated report is not necessarily a legal opinion. A qualified practitioner’s analysis also remains limited to the art found. It cannot guarantee that the USPTO will allow a claim or that another reference will not surface later. Invalidity search: $1,900–$10,000 in published pricing An invalidity search starts from an issued patent and selected claims. The searcher must identify the governing version of § 102, determine the effective filing date for each challenged claim, trace the relevant priority chains, and map each reference to what it discloses. For patent- or publication-based anticipation, a single enabling disclosure must disclose every claim limitation arranged as claimed, either expressly or inherently. Other § 102 categories, including public use, on-sale activity, and other public availability, can require different proof. An obviousness theory under § 103 may combine references, which adds another layer of technical and legal analysis. A publication-date cutoff does not capture every qualifying reference. For a challenged claim governed by the AIA’s first-inventor-to-file provisions, a U.S. patent, U.S. application publication, or qualifying WIPO publication may qualify under § 102(a)(2) even if it issues or publishes after the challenged claim’s effective filing date. The document must name another inventor, have been effectively filed before the challenged claim’s effective filing date for the relied-on subject matter, and fall outside the § 102(b)(2) exceptions. The USPTO states these rules in Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) § 2154 . Search scope should therefore capture publication and issue dates as well as inventive entities, actual filing, benefit, priority, and subject-matter-support data. Planet Patent publishes a $1,900–$10,000 average range for validity and invalidity searches in its average-price guide . Treat that as an indicative published average range, not a defined package price. The number of asserted claims, disputed priority issues, technical density, non-patent literature, product or system art, foreign-language material, and need for a claim chart can push a matter beyond it. A formal invalidity opinion, inter partes review petition, expert declaration, or litigation brief is separate work. Authorized practitioners can handle work within USPTO proceedings. Standalone litigation opinions require appropriately licensed attorneys, while court filings and appearances must follow the applicable court’s admission and pro se rules. USPTO registration alone is insufficient. The most valuable deliverable is rarely the longest reference list. It is a small set of strong references with dates, provenance, pinpoint citations, limitation mappings, and an auditable search trail. A coverage matrix also exposes gaps before counsel spends time polishing a weak reference. This is where AI changes the economics. It makes repeated search passes and early mappings cheap enough to run in-house, while attorneys retain control over priority, claim construction, evidentiary support, and the final invalidity theory. Our guide to AI prior art search tools explains the litigation-specific requirements in more depth. FTO search: $1,500–$3,000 for screening, with higher fees for opinions An FTO search answers a different question from patentability. Patentability asks what qualifying prior art may prevent you from patenting an invention. FTO asks whether making, using, selling, offering to sell, or importing a product in a specified country may fall within another party’s enforceable claims. Published search-only examples include a $1,500–$3,000 average range for infringement and FTO or clearance searches in Planet Patent’s guide . PRH charges a €2,670 base fee plus a mandatory €6.50 invoicing charge for its FTO service. Both charges are subject to 25.5% VAT, and PRH shows €3,359 as the total for its standard scope . That standard scope includes an initial meeting, about two days of examiner search work, a search report with legal-status information, and copies of the ten most relevant publications. PRH expressly does not take a position on possible infringement. Planet Patent’s figure is an indicative published average, while PRH’s total applies to its defined standard service. Published figures for higher-scope FTO work describe different purchases. Morse’s 2017 law-firm guidance places a formal FTO opinion at $10,000–$30,000. ipCapital Group’s 2026 cost analysis gives $10,000–$50,000 and beyond for a combined engagement spanning the search, analysis, and legal opinion, with the search and opinion treated as separate phases. The first figure is for the formal opinion; the second estimates the end-to-end engagement. The combined work can include searching, product-feature mapping, live-claim and legal-status analysis, and counsel’s written opinion. Analysts and patent agents can support search and mapping. When that support contributes to a legal opinion, it should be performed under the supervising licensed counsel responsible for the opinion. A U.S. FTO or noninfringement opinion should be issued by an appropriately licensed attorney authorized to provide that advice. USPTO registration is a separate credential for practice before the Office and is not always required for an FTO opinion. Qualified local counsel should be involved when other jurisdictions are in scope. The country and product boundaries must be explicit. Patent rights are territorial, legal status changes, and pending claims can change before issuance. A patent on your own improvement also does not confer permission to commercialize it. As WIPO explains in its freedom-to-operate guidance , a broader third-party patent may still cover the activity. Patent landscape: $800–$1,200 for a basic search, $5,000–$50,000+ for analysis A landscape is priced by the size of the field and the decision it needs to support. Planet Patent lists an $800–$1,200 average range for a broad-overview landscape search in its published guide . That basic output differs from a decision-focused analysis. ipCapital Group says scoped projects commonly run from about $5,000 for a narrow, single-technology review to $50,000 or more for a broad, multi-jurisdiction competitive landscape in its 2026 cost range . The higher-priced study may clean thousands of patent families, normalize assignees, read claims, categorize technologies, compare jurisdictions, and draw research and development or competitive conclusions. The two published ranges describe different deliverables rather than a single continuous market rate. A cheap landscape can still be useful when the question is narrow. It becomes expensive when the buyer expects high recall across a loosely defined field and human interpretation of every relevant family. Ask for the estimated document and family counts, inclusion rules, categorization depth, and update date before comparing landscape quotes. Why patent search costs vary Seven variables explain most price differences: The question. A quick novelty screen, a written patentability assessment, an invalidity theory, and an FTO opinion carry different stakes and analysis. The unit of work. One invention concept costs less than ten claims or a product with dozens of independently searchable features. Technical complexity. Chemical structures, biological sequences, standards, source code, and fast-changing terminology require specialized sources and search methods. Geographic scope. More countries add collections, languages, family consolidation, and legal-status review. Source coverage. Patents are only one source. Journals, standards, manuals, catalogs, theses, videos, archived web pages, and product evidence can require separate systems and verification. The deliverable. A list of publication numbers is cheaper than a ranked report with excerpts, claim mappings, pinpoint citations, search history, and attorney conclusions. Iteration and urgency. Extra search passes, newly identified claim constructions, and rush deadlines add cost. AI and in-house tools reduce the marginal cost of iteration most sharply. Technology labels alone are poor pricing proxies. A tightly scoped software claim can be easier than a deceptively simple mechanical assembly with decades of crowded art. The quote should describe the work, not merely name the field. Compare the total cost of using the results The lowest search invoice can create the highest matter cost. Use this formula: Total search cost = external or platform fee + internal review time + follow-on analysis or charting + paid reruns Suppose a $500 report returns a largely unranked set that takes a lawyer eight hours to screen. At a hypothetical $450 blended rate, the usable result costs $4,100 before any charting. A $2,000 report that reduces review to two hours costs $2,900 on the same assumptions. The arithmetic is illustrative, but the buying rule is real. Ask how the output reduces the next person’s work. For litigation, that usually means limitation-level mappings, pinpoint citations, and direct export into a review-ready claim chart . For prosecution, it means a concise set of close references that counsel can use when deciding whether and how to draft claims. For FTO, it means a defensible shortlist with current legal status and product-feature mappings. What every patent search quote should specify Use the same scope sheet for every bidder. A useful quote answers all of these questions: Question: Is the job a preliminary novelty check, patentability search, invalidity search, FTO analysis, infringement search, or landscape? Subject: Which invention disclosure, claims, product versions, features, or technology categories are included? Dates: Which version of § 102 governs, what effective filing date applies to each challenged claim, and who confirms the challenged and reference priority chains, public-availability dates, § 102(a)(2) effective-filing dates, inventive-entity differences, and applicable exceptions? Jurisdictions: Which patent offices and commercial markets are included? Sources: Are foreign patents, non-patent literature, standards, products, public-use evidence, and archived web materials in scope? Methods: Will the search use keywords, classifications, semantic search, citations, assignees, inventors, images, structures, or sequences? Deliverable: Will you receive raw references, relevance notes, excerpts, pinpoint citations, claim mappings, family data, legal status, and the query log? Review: Who performs quality control? Search-only patentability research does not require a registered practitioner. If the deliverable includes a patentability opinion or other legal advice about a USPTO matter, which registered patent attorney or agent is responsible? For an FTO, noninfringement, standalone validity, or court-litigation opinion, which licensed attorney is responsible? Iteration: How many feedback rounds or reruns are included, and what triggers an added fee? Operations: What are the turnaround time, confidentiality terms, data-retention terms, and total fixed or capped fee? If a provider cannot state what its price excludes, the quote is not ready to compare. Choose the budget that matches the decision Spend in stages when the stakes permit it: Run inexpensive triage. Use free public databases or an AI search to find obvious prior art and improve the vocabulary of the request. Pay for focused human review. Give the searcher or counsel a clear disclosure, known references, claims, dates, and markets. Better inputs prevent paid time from going toward basic scoping. Escalate only the strongest candidates. Commission a legal opinion, claim chart, expert work, or expanded jurisdictional search after the first pass shows where risk or value concentrates. Use a second method for high-stakes matters. For consequential litigation or product clearance, combine AI breadth and iteration with an independent expert search or counsel review. This staged model keeps a $50 screening question from turning into a $20,000 engagement too early. It also prevents a $50 report from being mistaken for the answer to a $20,000 legal question. Frequently asked questions Is a prior art search legally required before filing a patent application? No. The USPTO’s MPEP § 410 states that an applicant has no duty to conduct a prior art search before filing. The disclosure duty is separate. Under 37 C.F.R. § 1.56 , it applies to each inventor named in the application, each attorney or agent who prepares or prosecutes it, and every other person who is substantively involved in its preparation or prosecution and has the association specified in the rule. The rule does not categorically place that individual duty on applicant organizations. Whether a voluntary search is worth the cost depends on the invention, existing knowledge of the field, filing strategy, and budget. Can I do my own patent search? Yes. Public patent databases are free, and a DIY search is a sensible first screen. Use keywords and synonyms, CPC or International Patent Classification codes, backward and forward citations, foreign collections, and relevant non-patent literature. Treat the result as research, rather than a guarantee of patentability, validity, or freedom to operate. Can AI do a patent search? Yes. AI can search by technical concept, rank references, traverse citations, and map passages or figures to claim limitations. Its useful role is retrieval, triage, and drafting analysis for human review. A low-cost AI report is not automatically a legal opinion, and high-stakes conclusions remain with qualified counsel. How long does a patent search take? Most users of our Prior Art Search find strong candidate references within 30–60 minutes. That benchmark covers candidate discovery and excludes attorney review or a legal opinion. For its own novelty-search service, PRH says the search work typically takes one or a couple of working days. Its published delivery estimates are about two weeks for fixed-price work and three weeks for hourly work. WIPO’s 2015 guidelines reproduce a historical palm-oil landscape project schedule that assigned four weeks to Phase I, four weeks after comments to Phase II, and two weeks after comments to Phase III. That 2015 example is not a current WIPO service benchmark. Each timing applies only to its stated service, scope, or historical project. Does a patent search guarantee that no conflicting patent or prior art exists? No. Search terminology, classification, source access, translations, unpublished applications, and public evidence outside patent databases all create gaps. A well-scoped search reduces uncertainty and creates a better decision record. It cannot eliminate uncertainty. title: BorgWarner Reports Strong Second Quarter 2026 Results, Increases 2026 Adjusted EPS Guidance and Share Repurchase Authorization By $1 Billion, Announces 7 Awards Across Portfolio to Support Long-Term Profitable Growth
summary: Read and download our latest press releases.
body_text: Auburn Hills, Michigan, August 5, 2026 – BorgWarner Inc. (NYSE: BWA) today reported second quarter results for 2026. Second Quarter Results and Business Update BorgWarner’s (the “Company”) U.S. GAAP net sales increased approximately 0.3%, while organic net sales decreased approximately 1.2%, year-over-year compared with the second quarter of 2025. Excluding the decline in Battery Energy Systems segment sales of approximately $60 million, the Company’s organic net sales were up modestly year-over-year. The Company achieved a U.S. GAAP operating margin of 10.1% during the second quarter of 2026, or an increase of 220 basis points, compared with the second quarter of 2025. The Company achieved an adjusted operating margin of 11.3%, or an increase of 100 basis points, compared with the second quarter of 2025. The Company’s continued focus on cost controls allowed it to deliver strong performance despite a lower industry production environment. The Company repurchased approximately $100 million of its outstanding shares and paid a $34 million cash dividend to its shareholders during the second quarter of 2026. The Company’s Board of Directors authorized an increase to its share repurchase program of $1 billion, bringing the Company’s total authorization to approximately $1.35 billion, which is intended to allow management to repurchase the Company’s outstanding shares through 2029. The Company continued to make progress in its product readiness across its portfolio offerings for the data center and industrial markets. The Company plans to increase 2026 R&D spending to accelerate these future growth opportunities. New Business Awards Across Portfolio The Company secured multiple new business awards that are expected to support its long-term profitable growth, including the following: New eTurbo award with a major European OEM for an advanced hybrid passenger car application. Production is expected to begin in 2029. Torque-on-demand with mechanical lock transfer case award with a Chinese OEM for a newly developed, full-size SUV. Production is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026. Two variable cam timing awards. These include a conquest award with a major Chinese OEM and a program life extension award with a leading European premium OEM. Production is expected to begin in 2026 and 2027, respectively. Integrated Drive Modules (iDM) award with a global OEM. This program utilizes the Company’s next-generation iDM technology, setting a new benchmark in performance, efficiency and system integration. Production is expected to begin in 2027. Two high-volume inverter extension awards with a major European OEM for plug-in hybrid and 800V battery-electric vehicles. Production is expected to begin in 2029. Second Quarter Highlights: U.S. GAAP net sales of $3,648 million, an increase of approximately 0.3% compared with the second quarter of 2025. Excluding the impact of foreign currencies, organic net sales decreased 1.2% compared with the second quarter of 2025. U.S. GAAP net earnings of $1.34 per diluted share. Excluding $0.08 of net losses per diluted share related to non-comparable items (detailed in the table below), adjusted net earnings were $1.42 per diluted share, an increase of 17.4% compared with the second quarter of 2025. U.S. GAAP operating income of $370 million, or 10.1% of net sales. Excluding $43 million of pretax expenses related to non-comparable items, adjusted operating income was $413 million, or 11.3% of net sales. Net cash provided by operating activities of $586 million. Free cash flow of $492 million. Financial Results: The Company believes the following table is useful in highlighting non-comparable items that impacted its U.S. GAAP net earnings per diluted share. The non-comparable items presented below are calculated after tax using the corresponding effective tax rate discrete to each item and the weighted average number of diluted shares for the periods presented. The Company defines adjusted earnings per diluted share as earnings per diluted share adjusted to eliminate the impact of restructuring expense, merger, acquisition and divestiture expense, other net expenses, discontinued operations and other gains and losses not reflective of the Company’s ongoing operations and related tax effects. Net sales were $3,648 million for the second quarter of 2026, an increase of approximately 0.3% compared with the second quarter of 2025. This increase was due to stronger foreign currencies compared to the U.S. dollar, partially offset by declining market production volumes and lower Battery Energy Systems segment sales. Net earnings for the second quarter of 2026 were $277 million, compared with net earnings of $224 million for the second quarter of 2025. Net earnings per share for the second quarter of 2026 were $1.34 per diluted share, up 30.1% from $1.03 per diluted share for the second quarter of 2025. Adjusted net earnings per diluted share for the second quarter of 2026 were $1.42, up 17.4% from adjusted net earnings per diluted share of $1.21 for the second quarter of 2025. Adjusted net earnings for the second quarter of 2026 excluded net non-comparable items of $(0.08) per diluted share, while adjusted net earnings for the second quarter of 2025 excluded net non-comparable items of $(0.18) per diluted share. These and other non-comparable items are listed in the table above, which is provided by the Company for comparison with other results and the most directly comparable U.S. GAAP measures. The increase in adjusted net earnings per diluted share was primarily due to higher adjusted operating income and the impact of a lower share count as a result of 2025 and 2026 share repurchases. Full Year 2026 Guidance Update: The Company increased its 2026 full year adjusted earnings per share guidance, while maintaining its sales, adjusted operating margin and cash flow expectations. At the mid-point of its 2026 guidance, the Company expects to deliver another year of adjusted operating margin improvement and adjusted earnings per share growth despite the Company’s expectation that its weighted light vehicle markets will be down 3% to approximately flat and a decline in the Company’s Battery Energy Systems segment sales. Net sales are expected to be in the range of $14.0 billion to $14.3 billion in 2026, compared with 2025 net sales of approximately $14.3 billion. The Company’s net sales guidance implies a year-over-year change in organic net sales of down 3.5% to down 1.5%. The Company’s net sales guidance includes an expected year-over-year sales decline of approximately $250 million in the Company’s Battery Energy Systems segment, which represents approximately a 1.7% headwind to organic net sales growth in 2026. Foreign currencies are expected to result in a year-over-year increase in sales of approximately $175 million primarily due to the strengthening of the Euro and Chinese Renminbi against the U.S. dollar. U.S. GAAP operating margin is expected to be in the range of 9.6% to 9.8% in 2026. Excluding the impact of non-comparable items and the add back of intangible asset amortization expense, adjusted operating margin is expected to be in the range of 10.7% to 10.9%. U.S. GAAP net earnings are expected to be within the range of $4.72 to $4.94 per diluted share. Excluding the impact of noncomparable items, adjusted net earnings are expected to be in the range of $5.05 to $5.30 per diluted share, compared to the Company’s previous adjusted net earnings range of $5.00 to $5.20 per diluted share. The increase is due to the impact of the Company’s share repurchases during the first half of 2026. Full year operating cash flow is expected to be in the range of $1,600 million to $1,700 million, while free cash flow is expected to be in the range of $900 million to $1,100 million. At 9:30 a.m. ET today, a brief conference call concerning second quarter 2026 results and full year guidance will be webcast at: https://www.borgwarner.com/investors . Additionally, an earnings call presentation will be available at https://www.borgwarner.com/investors .

title: BWX Technologies Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results
summary: 2Q26 revenues of $901.6 million 2Q26 net income of $89.1 million, adjusted EBITDA (1) of $155.5 million 2Q26 diluted GAAP EPS of $0.97, non-GAAP (1) EPS of $1.07 Announced the sale of the medical business, enabling increased focus on core nuclear national defense and commercial nuclear power
body_text: BWX Technologies Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results August 3, 2026 PDF Version 2Q26 revenues of $901.6 million 2Q26 net income of $89.1 million, adjusted EBITDA(1) of $155.5 million 2Q26 diluted GAAP EPS of $0.97, non-GAAP(1) EPS of $1.07 Announced the sale of the medical business, enabling increased focus on core nuclear national defense and commercial nuclear power markets Closed the acquisition of Precision Components Group, LLC (PCG) on July 1, 2026, establishing a U.S. footprint for commercial nuclear component manufacturing Raising adjusted EBITDA(1) guidance to $662 million-$672 million, non-GAAP EPS(1) guidance to $4.70-$4.80, and free cash flow(1) guidance to $345 million-$360 million LYNCHBURG, Va.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 3, 2026-- BWX Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: BWXT) ("BWXT", "we", "us" or the "Company") reported second quarter 2026 results. A reconciliation of non-GAAP results is detailed in Exhibit 1. “We had strong second quarter 2026 results that were ahead of our expectations,” said Rex. D. Geveden, president and chief executive officer. “Once again we saw strong execution across our business, high growth in Commercial Operations, and good free cash flow generation.” “Demand for new nuclear solutions is remarkably deep and broad, complementing our strong and growing base of highly predictable revenue streams in our Government and Commercial segments,” continued Geveden. “In line with our strategy to bolster BWXT’s competitive positioning in the nuclear national security and commercial nuclear power markets, the announced sale of our medical business enables us to increase focus and resources in these core business lines. This strategy is already in action through our commercial manufacturing expansion in the U.S. and ongoing investments to drive capacity and modernization across our manufacturing footprint.” “Reflecting our strong first half performance, contribution from the recently completed PCG acquisition, and confidence in our execution over the remainder of the year, we are raising our 2026 financial guidance,” said Geveden. “We now anticipate adjusted EBITDA of $662 million-$672 million, non-GAAP EPS of $4.70-$4.80, and $345 million-$360 million of free cash flow.” (1) A reconciliation of non-GAAP results are detailed in Exhibit 1. The Government Operations increase was driven by growth in naval propulsion and special materials, partially offset lower advanced nuclear volumes. BWXT believes the non-GAAP measures provide meaningful insight and transparency into the Company’s operational performance and provides these measures to investors to help facilitate comparisons of operating results with prior periods and to assist them in understanding BWXT's ongoing operations. Definitions for the non-GAAP measures are provided below and reconciliations are detailed in Exhibit 1, except that reconciliations of forward-looking GAAP measures are not provided because the company is unable to reliably forecast most of the items that are excluded from GAAP to calculate non-GAAP results. Other companies may define these measures differently or may utilize different non-GAAP measures, thus impacting comparability. Non-GAAP Earnings Per Share (EPS) is calculated using GAAP EPS less the non-operational tax effected per share impact of pension & OPEB mark-to-market gains or losses and other one-time items, such as restructuring, transformation, acquisition-related costs, and acquisition-related amortization. Adjusted Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EBITDA) is calculated using non-GAAP net income, plus provision for income taxes, less other – net, less interest income, plus interest expense, plus depreciation and amortization. Adjusted pre-tax income is non-GAAP income before provision for income taxes. Free Cash Flow (FCF) is calculated using net income to derive net cash provided by (used in) operating activities less purchases of property, plant and equipment. Free Cash Flow conversion is free cash flow divided by net income. title: Introducing the Life Sciences Category in Firecrawl Research Index

body_text: Today we're launching the Life Sciences category in the Firecrawl Research Index . It covers 41M+ papers across the drug discovery, clinical trial, and biology literature. title: From Around the Moon to Canoga Park: Artemis II Crew Visits L3Harris Following Historic Mission
summary: L3Harris welcomed the Artemis II crew and NASA leaders to the Los Angeles site in Canoga Park to celebrate the successful Artemis II mission.
body_text: Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, visit the L3Harris site in Los Angeles following successful completion of the Artemis II mission. Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christ... Editorial From Around the Moon to Canoga Park: Artemis II Crew Visits L3Harris Following Historic Mission L3Harris welcomed the Artemis II crew and NASA leaders to the Los Angeles site in Canoga Park to celebrate the successful Artemis II mission. MS Missile Solutions Aug 19, 2026 | 3 MINUTE Read SHARE Facebook Linkedin X Space Missile Solutions Civil Space Space Solutions In-Space Power & Propulsion Liquid Engines SHARE Facebook Linkedin X Just months after the Artemis II crew made history, surpassing the record for human spaceflight’s farthest distance from Earth, members of the Artemis II crew and NASA leadership are visiting suppliers who helped make the journey possible. They recently traveled to L3Harris’ Canoga Park site, home of the storied RS-25 engines, to express their gratitude to employees who have dedicated their careers to building the technology that helps launch astronauts into orbit safely. The four members of the Artemis II crew – Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover and Mission Specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen – were welcomed to the site with thunderous cheers from nearly 1,000 L3Harris employees who gathered to celebrate their achievements and the hard work of NASA and its industry. In his opening remarks, L3Harris Missile Solutions President Ken Bedingfield told the Canoga Park team he was humbled to represent them, noting we are here “to honor and recognize the incredible work each of you did in ensuring the successful Artemis II mission.” He referenced Christina Koch’s previous remarks on the importance of a crew – one “that is stroking together every minute with the same purpose” and that “holds [one other] accountable.” Bedingfield noted that the Canoga Park team “is our crew.” “It’s incredibly motivating to welcome these astronauts who just made history to our site,” said Scott Alexander, President, Propulsion Systems, Missile Solutions, L3Harris. “Whenever the end user of our technology, whether a warfighter or an astronaut, meets with our teams in person, it underscores the impact and critical importance of the work our teams do every day.” NASA leaders presented L3Harris with an item flown in space as a token of appreciation for the company’s contributions to the successful Artemis II mission. Pictured from L to R: Dr. Sharon Cobb, Acting Deputy Program Manager, SLS, NASA; Johnny Heflin, Manager, Liquid Engines Element, NASA; Ken Bedingfield, President, Missile Solutions, L3Harris; Mike Lauer, General Manager and Program Manager, RS-25 SLS, L3Harris; and Dr. Lori Glaze, Associate Administrator, Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate, NASA. NASA leaders presented L3Harris with an item flown in space ... During the visit, NASA leaders presented an Artemis II flag flown in space to Bedingfield and Mike Lauer, General Manager and Program Manager, RS-25 SLS, who accepted it on behalf of the company. The recognition honored L3Harris for “significant contributions, exemplary performance and dedication to NASA in the successful launch of the Artemis II mission.” L3Harris supplied significant capabilities for the historic space mission that captivated the world, including propulsion systems, communications and avionics. The RS-25 engines, which generated 2 million pounds of thrust during the Artemis II mission, powered NASA’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket for the first eight and a half minutes of flight into orbit. “Words can’t fully express the honor and gratitude the RS-25 team felt in hosting the Artemis II crew,” said Mike Lauer, General Manager and Program Manager, RS-25 SLS, Missile Solutions, L3Harris. “Those four astronauts are outstanding role models, demonstrating how teamwork makes it possible to accomplish the most difficult challenges. That same ethic is one the RS-25 team at L3Harris embraces and strives to uphold every day.” The Artemis II crew leads an “integrity” cheer with L3Harris Canoga Park employees. The Artemis II crew leads an “integrity” cheer with L3Harris... For six decades, L3Harris has proudly supported NASA with technologies essential to the evolution of lunar exploration, sending astronauts to the moon’s surface and beyond. Just last month, L3Harris reached another key milestone: the delivery of the four RS‑25 engines that will power Artemis III. For Kevin McCombs, Vice President and General Manager, Strategic Systems, L3Harris, the visit highlighted the pride and momentum behind the company’s continued support for NASA’s Artemis program. “The legacy of the RS‑25 engines continues to guide L3Harris’ commitment to the advancement of human spaceflight," said McCombs. "We deliver propulsion solutions for the world’s most complex and critical missions. Our dedicated workforce is driving modernization and leveraging advanced production processes to support future Artemis missions with greater speed and efficiency." As NASA prepares for Artemis III and the missions that will follow, the L3Harris team remains committed to doing its part to advance the future of human exploration, so astronauts can travel farther than ever before. title: Definium Therapeutics Announces New Employee Inducement Grants
summary: NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Definium Therapeutics, Inc. (“Definium” or the “Company”), a late-stage clinical biopharmaceutical company…...
body_text: Definium Therapeutics Announces New Employee Inducement Grants August 03, 2026 4:01pm EDT Download as PDF NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Definium Therapeutics, Inc. (“Definium” or the “Company”), a late-stage clinical biopharmaceutical company developing a new generation of therapeutics intended to address underlying causes of psychiatric and neurological disorders, today announced the issuance of inducement grants to six newly hired non-executive employees consisting of options to purchase an aggregate of 115,600 common shares of the Company (the "Options") with effective grant dates of August 3, 2026. The Options have an exercise price equal to the closing price of Definium’s common shares on the date of the grants, and will vest over a four-year period with 25% vesting on the first anniversary of the date of the grant and the remaining 75% vesting in substantially equal monthly increments over the three-year period thereafter, subject to each employee’s continued employment. The Options were granted as a material inducement to each employee’s employment and were approved by Definium’s Compensation Committee on August 2, 2026, in accordance with Rule 5635(c)(4) of The NASDAQ Stock Market LLC. The Options were granted pursuant to Definium’s 2026 Inducement Plan. About Definium Therapeutics The mission of Definium Therapeutics is to forge a new era of psychiatry by applying scientific rigor to psychedelics, with the goal of developing accessible treatments that unlock healing at scale. Guided by a recognition that patients deserve more than better, Definium is relentlessly advancing a new generation of therapeutics intended to address underlying causes of psychiatric and neurological disorders. By turning evidence into impact, Definium aims to change the trajectory of today’s mental health care crisis and enable a healthier future.
